lines.text: For over four thousand years, rulers have tried to bind many peoples under one crown. These are the great empires of history, how they rose and how they fell.
It begins in Mesopotamia, with Sargon of Akkad, who joined the Sumerian cities to lands beyond them and made the first empire.
On the upper Tigris, Assyria grew into the largest empire of its age, with a feared army and a great library at Nineveh.
Far to the west, Phoenician settlers founded Carthage on the coast of Africa. It would become a rich sea power, and Rome's great rival.
In northern Greece, the kingdom of Macedon was rising. Under Alexander the Great it would bring down Persia itself.
Cyrus the Great founded the first Persian empire, from Egypt to the Indus, held together by governors, a royal road and tolerance of local ways.
Meanwhile Rome threw out its kings. As a republic of senators and elected officials, it won Italy and then the whole Mediterranean.
In India, Chandragupta Maurya united most of the subcontinent for the first time. His grandson Ashoka spread Buddhism and carved his laws in stone.
In China the Han ruled for about four centuries, opening the Silk Road, training officials in Confucian learning, and inventing paper.
Rome's generals fought until Augustus took power. Under its emperors, Rome stretched from Britain to Egypt, spreading roads, law and Latin.
Persia rose again under the Sasanians, rivals of Rome for four centuries, whose silver, silk and buildings shaped later Islamic art.
In northern India, the Gupta age became a golden time for science and verse, when scholars worked on zero and the decimal system.
When the west of Rome fell, the east lived on. From Constantinople, Byzantium kept Greek learning and Roman law alive for a thousand years.
Under the Tang, China reached a high point of culture, its capital Chang'an full of traders from the Silk Road and poets like Li Bai.
Out of Arabia, a new faith built a new empire. The Umayyads ruled from Damascus, from Spain to the edge of India.
The Abbasids moved the capital to Baghdad, where the House of Wisdom translated Greek texts and pushed forward mathematics and medicine.
In Cambodia, the Khmer kings ruled from Angkor, raising hundreds of temples, Angkor Wat among them, above a vast web of canals.
In Europe, Otto the First was crowned emperor, and the Holy Roman Empire began, a loose patchwork that would last eight hundred years.
Then out of the steppe came Genghis Khan. His Mongols built the largest land empire ever, from Korea to Eastern Europe.
In West Africa, Sundiata Keita founded Mali, rich in gold. Its ruler Mansa Musa made a legendary pilgrimage to Mecca.
In a corner of Anatolia, a Turkish leader named Osman led a small band. His family would found an empire.
The Ottoman Empire grew to hold south-eastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, its sultans reigning for over six hundred years.
China threw off the Mongols, and the Ming built much of the Great Wall we see today, the Forbidden City, and great fleets under Zheng He.
In 1415 Portugal seized Ceuta in North Africa. Its trading posts would ring Africa, India and Brazil, the first European global empire.
Across the ocean, three cities in central Mexico formed the Aztec alliance, led by Tenochtitlan, a great city built on a lake.
Mehmed the Second became sultan young, and at twenty-one set out to take the greatest prize of all.
In the Andes, the Inca built the largest empire of the Americas, linked by mountain roads, from Ecuador to Chile.
In 1453, after a siege of about two months, Constantinople fell to the Ottomans. The thousand-year Byzantine Empire was gone.
In their new capital, the sultans built Topkapi Palace, their home and seat of government for four hundred years.
Selim the First conquered Egypt, Syria and the holy cities of Arabia, and doubled the empire's size.
Meanwhile Columbus had reached the Americas. Spain's empire would hold much of the New World, and its silver would move world trade.
Under Suleiman the Magnificent, the Ottomans reached their height, taking Belgrade and Rhodes, and reforming the law.
In India, Babur founded the Mughal Empire. His heirs would build the Taj Mahal and blend Persian and Indian culture.
In 1529 Suleiman laid siege to Vienna, and failed. It marked the high tide of the Ottoman advance into Europe.
At home the architect Sinan raised the Suleymaniye Mosque for him, crowning a hill above Istanbul.
In 1571, off western Greece, a fleet led by Spain and Venice defeated the Ottoman navy, in one of the last great battles of oared galleys.
England, late to the race, began claiming lands overseas. The British Empire would grow into the largest the world has ever seen.
In 1600 a trading company was chartered in London. In time the East India Company would rule much of India with its own army.
In 1607 English settlers founded Jamestown in Virginia, their first lasting foothold in America.
In Istanbul, the Blue Mosque rose with its six minarets, facing Hagia Sophia across a square.
In China, the Manchus founded the Qing, the last imperial dynasty, and pushed the empire to its greatest size.
In 1683 the Ottomans besieged Vienna again. A relief army under the Polish king broke the siege, and the long Ottoman retreat began.
Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire, which spread across Siberia into Central Asia, one of the largest states on Earth.
In 1757, at Plassey, the Company's forces under Robert Clive won Bengal, and British rule in India began.
But Britain lost thirteen colonies in America. With French help, they won their independence as the United States.
Britain looked elsewhere. In 1788 eleven ships reached Botany Bay, and the colonisation of Australia began.
Queen Victoria would reign over sixty-three years, Empress of India, at the centre of an empire on which the sun never set.
In 1833 Britain ended slavery across most of its empire, paying the owners large sums while the freed people got nothing.
When China banned the opium trade, Britain went to war, and took Hong Kong as its prize.
The Ottomans, now falling behind, tried to modernise their laws, army and schools on European lines.
In 1857 Indian soldiers rose against the Company, and the revolt spread across northern India before it was crushed.
The British Crown took India directly. The Raj built railways, but also saw famines and a growing call for independence.
In central Europe, the Habsburgs joined Austria and Hungary in a dual monarchy of many peoples.
Japan modernised at astonishing speed and built an empire of its own, taking Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria.
In 1871, at Versailles, a new German Empire was proclaimed, soon an industrial and military giant.
Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman officer, would one day build a new Turkey from the empire's ruins.
In a few decades the European powers carved up almost all of Africa. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed free.
In southern Africa, Britain fought the Boer republics, and won only after a bitter guerrilla war and camps that held civilians.
In 1908 Ottoman officers forced the sultan to bring back the constitution and parliament.
In the First World War, the Ottoman government deported and killed vast numbers of Armenians, hundreds of thousands or more.
At Gallipoli, the Allies tried to knock the Ottomans out of the war, and failed after months of fighting.
In 1922 the Turkish parliament abolished the sultanate. Over six hundred years of Ottoman rule were over.
The Russian Empire fell to revolution, and in its place rose the Soviet Union, a communist superpower, until it too fell in 1991.
Britain's empire began to change shape, into a free association of nations, the Commonwealth.
In 1931 Canada, Australia and the other dominions won full power to make their own laws.
In 1947 British India became independent as India and Pakistan. Millions crossed the new borders, and terrible violence followed.
In 1956 Britain and France attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal, and were forced to back down, a sign their imperial day was done.
In 1960 Harold Macmillan spoke of a wind of change, accepting that Africa's colonies would be free.
And in 1997, after a hundred and fifty-six years, Britain handed Hong Kong back to China.
Every empire believed it would last forever, and every one of them, in the end, gave way.
